opener.heading: Week 35: Music & Movement 🎵
about: Every day this week Azlyn makes a noise she is in charge of. Five pots get numerals taped to their fronts on Friday and she plays the row by walking down it. Saturday runs with the curtains shut and a flashlight in her fist. Sunday puts the three of you on six feet of paper with a song telling you when to move up one place, Monday she builds a museum out of six things that bang and gives the tour herself, and Tuesday she drives two screws into a wooden ruler with a real screwdriver, and taped to a cookie tin it comes out a guitar. Most days the morning makes the thing and the afternoon plays it.
No holiday lands in the week. Wednesday is September 1, so the month turns in the middle of it.
Heat is the thing to plan around. Most of the Get Outside walks are written for shade or for the cooler end of the day, and Tuesday is swimming, which is the coldest room she will stand in all week.
azlyn: Numerals as shapes. She matches a printed 1 to 5 against the pot wearing the same mark, months before the numeral stands for a quantity.
Where a sound is coming from. Loud corner, quiet corner, a timer ticking under a cushion, and a jar of rice telling her warm or cold.
A real screwdriver. The wrist turn, elbow tucked in, and a screw that goes home under her own hand.
Taking a turn in a circle. One spoon decides who sings, and she can see her turn coming round the ring before it arrives.
Her shadow answers to her feet. Walk towards the lamp and it fills the sheet, walk back to the sheet and it comes down to her own size.
you: Numeral recognition is separate from counting
Darkness is worth practicing when it isn't bedtime
A large collaborative piece teaches something a small one can't
Explaining it to a stranger sends her back through it another way
Real tools and real jobs beat toy versions, every time
Sitting in a circle changes how a group talks
She's met shadows three times now, and each time added something

days.title: Music You Can Read
days.prepTonight: Cut twenty cards the size of a playing card from a cereal box and leave them blank in a stack with the permanent marker and the masking tape.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: The Five Loudest Things in the Kitchen

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Cards Left on the Floor

opening.title: The Five Loudest Things in the Kitchen
opening.need: the pan cabinet · masking tape · 1 permanent marker · 1 wooden spoon.
steps: Open the cabinet and let her hit whatever she can reach with the spoon. Loud is the point for the first few minutes.
Keep five that sound different and stand them in a row on the floor, loudest at one end.
Tape a strip across the front of each and write 1 to 5 along the row. She says each number out loud as the marker makes it.

main.title: Playing What the Cards Say
materials: 5 saucepans, tins or plastic tubs that sound different, taped and numbered this morning
20 cards cut from a cereal box, numerals 1 to 5, four of each
steps: Sit the five in a row on the floor and run a strip of masking tape along the front of them, so every pot has a place to go back to.
Write the numerals on the twenty blank cards with the marker, four of each, and let her call out the ones she knows. Stack them face down.
Turn one over and hold it up. She finds the pot wearing that numeral and hits it once with a spoon. If she picks wrong, hold your card next to the tape on the pot and let her compare the shapes.
Run ten cards through, then go faster until she gets there before the card is upright.
Take the second spoon and swap jobs. She holds the cards up, you play, and she will hold up a 2 and watch whether you cheat.
Let her lay four cards in a row. Play that row left to right twice, then hand her the spoon and let her play her own song back.
main.tip: She is matching the numeral as a shape long before it means five of anything. Hold the card beside the pot instead of saying the number.

outside.title: Where the Grasshoppers Are Loudest
paras: Late August has one sound in it, and it comes out of the long grass at the warmest part of the morning. Walk to three patches you can get close to, a verge, a hedge bottom, the rough end of the park, and stop at each for a slow count of ten. The grasshoppers and crickets cut out as you arrive and start up again once she holds still, so the standing still is the whole skill. One patch will be loud enough that you have to raise your voice. Ask her which one wins.

days.infant: Kreston is 14 months and has three to five words. At the edge of the grass he stops walking the moment the noise starts: hear a thing, stop, hunt for where it came from. Point down into the stems. He will not find them and he will keep looking.

second.title: The Song You Walk On
second.intro: After lunch the five pots go down the hallway in a line and she plays the row by walking it.
materials: Chalk, if the line goes out onto the path
steps: Run a line of masking tape down the middle of the hallway, as long as the hall gives you.
Stand the five pots along the line a stride apart, in whatever order she puts them.
Lay one card face up in front of each pot. Card numeral and pot numeral have to match, and she checks the row before anybody plays it.
She walks the line with the spoon, hitting each pot as she reaches it. Read the numbers out loud behind her as she goes.
Send her back the other way. Same pots, same cards, and the song comes out backwards.
Let her move two pots and swap two cards, then play the new line. Twenty minutes of it is normal, and she comes back to it after a break.
If the hall is too short, take the lot out to the path and chalk the line instead.
second.tip: Walk it slow once and fast once. Same pots, same order, and it comes out a different song.

alternatives: Three pots and three cards, no line, on the kitchen floor.
Sort all twenty cards into five piles and stop there.
Tape the cards up the stairs, one per step, and count them going up.
Play the row on the pans while she conducts with both arms.
outAgain: Grandparents or family, and she takes four cards and one pot to show them
The shady half of the park, and home before the worst of the heat
A friend's garden, where the pots can be as loud as they like
The corner store for something cold, counting five things into the basket
The paddling pool in the yard, with the numbered pots refilled as buckets

aroundWorld.title: Rhythms of the World 🥁
paras: Much of the world's music runs on a short pattern that repeats under everything else. Cuban bands lock to the clave, five strokes across two bars that the whole band hears whether or not anyone plays it. Ghanaian drummers hold a bell pattern for the same reason, and Indian classical music counts long cycles called tala out on the fingers.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Chopped mango and milk in a lidded jar, shaken to the clave: three shakes, a gap, then two. Azlyn holds the jar and you count her in.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Clave is Spanish for key, and the pattern is the key the rest of the band unlocks itself with.

days.krestonPM: Give him a plastic tub and a spoon at the far end of the hall, well away from the metal. At 14 months he stacks two blocks and he will try to stack the tub on a pot. He carries the cards off one at a time, so count them back in.

insight.headline: Numeral recognition is separate from counting.
paras: Azlyn can count five spoons onto the table and still have no idea what a printed 5 is, and the two skills sit in different places. Counting is a physical routine: one object, one word, one touch. Reading a numeral is shape recognition, the same machinery she uses on a stop sign or the first letter of her name, and it arrives on its own schedule. Pairing them the way today does, card in one hand and the pot wearing the same mark under the other, stitches the two together over months. She does not need quizzing. She needs to see them side by side, often.

days.safety: Opened tins keep a rim sharp enough to cut, so run your thumb round every one first and use a plastic tub where the edge worries you. Metal banged at close range is loud enough to hurt Kreston's ears at 14 months. Keep him a good stride back, or out of the room for the fast rounds. The grass hunt runs at the warmest part of the morning, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

days.title: Dancing in the Dark
days.prepTonight: Put fresh batteries in two or three flashlights, cut two squares out of a colored plastic folder, and leave them with the candy wrappers, the rubber bands and a dark blanket.

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: The Cold Drinks Into the Bag

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Bath With the Big Light Off

opening.title: Coloring the Flashlight Beams
opening.need: 2 or 3 flashlights · candy wrappers or colored tissue · rubber bands · masking tape.
steps: Switch each flashlight on and off in her hand and put aside any with a tired yellow beam.
Stretch a wrapper over the front of each flashlight and hold it there with a rubber band. Two layers give a stronger color.
Tape the loose ends flat against the barrel so nothing hangs across the lens. Stand the flashlights in a row, switched off, until quarter past nine.

main.title: Dancing With the Lights Off
materials: 2 or 3 flashlights with fresh batteries, colored this morning
Candy wrappers or colored tissue, plus the 2 plastic folder squares, for spare lenses
Rubber bands and 1 roll masking tape
A phone or radio for music
steps: Tape the dark blanket across the brightest window, corner by corner, and pull the curtains over the top. Give the room a minute; it never goes as dark as she expects.
One flashlight each. Music on, loud enough to come up through the floor.
Dance. Beams on the ceiling, along the walls, across each other. No rules for the first two songs.
Stop the music without warning. Everybody freezes and points at one spot on the ceiling, so the colors land together.
Start and stop six or seven more times. Between two of the songs, switch every flashlight off and stand in the dark for ten seconds.
Big light on to trade lenses. Pull the rubber bands off, band a plastic square on where a wrapper has torn, then lights off again for the last song in somebody else's color.
main.tip: Freeze when the music stops rather than dropping. Holding still in the dark with a beam on the ceiling is harder than the dancing.

outside.title: The Noisiest Place and the Quietest
paras: Go before the heat sets in, with water. Stand at the busiest corner you can reach for a slow count of twenty, naming what you hear. Then let her lead you to the quietest place she knows and count twenty again.

days.infant: Kreston is 14 months and walking everywhere. At the loud corner he will grip your hand harder without once looking away, a fourteen-month-old sorting a big noise out for himself. Give him the full twenty seconds.

second.title: Following the Sound With a Flashlight
second.intro: Curtains go across again after lunch. She walks the house on her ears, and the flashlight confirms what she worked out.
materials: A phone playing something quiet on a loop
1 squeaky toy, or 1 bell taped to the back of a chair
The hiding places: 1 shoe, 1 sofa cushion, 1 folded towel, the laundry basket
steps: Draw the curtains through the downstairs and turn the big lights off. Aim for dim rather than pitch black.

Park her at the bottom of the stairs with a flashlight, counting to twenty out loud, while you hide three sounds: the timer wound up on a low shelf, the phone under a sofa cushion, and the squeaky toy inside a shoe.
Send her hunting. You keep the jar of rice and shake it fast when she is close, slow when she is heading the wrong way.
She brings each one back as she finds it. Wind the timer up again before it runs out of tick.
Hide the same three harder. Behind a door, under a folded towel, inside the laundry basket.
Round three belongs to her. She hides all three and shakes the jar while you hunt, and her warm and cold will be nonsense. Follow it anyway.
Finish with the curtains open and everything found again in the light.
second.tip: Hide nothing above her head height. A sound on top of a closet takes the deciding away from her.

alternatives: One sound hidden in one room, found ten times over.
Everyone sits still with eyes shut and names five sounds in the house.
A den made from the dark blanket, flashlights inside.
Hand shapes on the wall with one flashlight, sitting still.
outAgain: The aquarium, dim rooms and lit tanks, which is this morning turned inside out
The shady woodland path, and take a flashlight for the dark bits
The park at half past four, once the sun is off the equipment
The afternoon showing at the movie theater, the darkest room in town
days.krestonPM: At 14 months he scribbles, and a flashlight beam on the floor reads to him as a mark he can chase. Hold the flashlight and walk the spot along the carpet at his pace. At the aquarium he will stand at one tank tracking a single fish.

insight.headline: Darkness is worth practicing when it isn't bedtime.
paras: Three is the age fear of the dark tends to arrive, and it arrives at 7:30 at night when everybody is tired and nobody can do much about it. A dark room at ten in the morning, with music on and a flashlight in her fist, gives Azlyn the same information under conditions she controls. She learns what the room does to sound, that the shapes stay where they were, that dark ends when she flicks a switch. All of it transfers as a body memory of being in the dark and being fine, which she reaches for at bedtime without knowing where it came from.

days.safety: Small flashlights run on button batteries, which are the worst thing a 14-month-old can swallow. Check every battery door is screwed or clipped shut before Kreston is in the room, and never leave a loose flashlight on the floor. He is walking now, so clear the floor of toys, bags and cables before the lights go off. Rubber bands and wrappers are choking size, so put the big light on to trade lenses between songs and count every loose band back into your pocket before the room goes dark again. The corner and the walk to it are in open sun, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

days.title: The Long Painting
days.prepTonight: Flatten six boxes and stack them by the hall door, or stand the roll of butcher paper against the wall, and put the paints, plastic cups and two old towels beside them.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: Putting It Up Along the Hall

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Warm Bath and the Paint Off Her Arms

opening.title: Rolling Out the Long Paper
opening.need: 1 roll of butcher paper, or 6 flattened boxes · packing tape.
steps: Give her the end of the roll and let her walk it down the hall while you feed it out behind her. With boxes, lay them end to end and tape every seam on both sides.
Tape the paper to the floor along both edges, a strip every arm's length. She presses each one down.
Walk the length counting her steps. That number is how long the painting is.

main.title: Everybody Paints at Once
materials: The taped-down butcher paper, or 6 flattened boxes taped end to end
Washable non-toxic poster paint in 3 colors
A phone or radio for music
steps: Split the length into three stretches, one for you, one for Azlyn and one for Kreston at the end nearest the door. Kneel down at your own with one brush and one color each, and tape a plastic cup of water on the wall side of your place and hers with a loop of packing tape, out past where Kreston kneels, so a knee cannot tip it. He works off yours.
Music on. Everyone paints their own stretch.

Stop the music. Stand up, move one stretch along, kneel down and carry on in your own color on somebody else's work. Whoever is at the far end walks back to the start, and Kreston stays where he is, still working off your cup.
Run it four or five times. She will get precious about her bit at the first move and stop caring by the third.
Pass the sponge round for the last song. Pressed flat and lifted, it puts down a texture no brush makes.
Wipe hands on the towels, leave it taped to the floor to dry, and shut the hall door on it until one o'clock.
main.tip: Keep one color per person for the whole hour. Three colors crossing over each other is what stops the whole thing going brown.

outside.title: Playing the Railings
paras: Take a stick and play the street on the way to the store. Railings give a run of clicks, a trash can one flat thump, a metal gate rings, and a fence panel does nothing at all. Run the stick slow then fast along the same railings. Ask her why the dead fence has no sound in it.

days.infant: Kreston is 14 months. Give him a short stick of his own and let him hit the railings at his own height. He is at the stage of banging one thing on another to hear what comes out, and the railings run a hundred feet of that.

second.title: Putting It Up Along the Hall
second.intro: Up on the wall at her eye height, the painting is a thing the family walks past twenty times a day.
materials: A phone or radio for music
steps: Peel it off the floor together and walk its whole length once, flat, before anything gets cut.
Ask her where it should live, then cut it into wall-length sections with your scissors while she holds the far end steady.
Tape the sections up along the hall at her eye height, not yours. Masking tape rolled into loops behind the corners comes off the paint again later.
Take the marker. She dictates and you write: whose stretch this was, what it turned into after the third swap, the bit she says is a storm.
Carry on round the corner and up the stairs if there is more painting than hall.
Music on, the same songs as this morning, and walk the length of it naming who painted what.
Photograph it from floor level at one end, the one place it looks as long as it is.
second.tip: Hang it low enough that Kreston can reach the bottom edge. Retaping what he pulls down costs less than a painting she cannot get at.

alternatives: Fold it into a concertina book instead and read it page by page.
Cut one square out of the best bit and tape it to the fridge.
Leave it on the floor and drive cars along it.
Paint a second short one outside on a flattened box.
outAgain: A nature hunt walk, one bag, and everything she brings back gets taped to the painting
The long field loop while the grass is still dry
The playground at five, once the metal has cooled off
Feeding the ducks with oats or defrosted peas, never bread
The garden center, cool inside, and one packet of seeds to plant this week
days.krestonPM: At 14 months he scribbles, so give him his own square of the offcut on the floor and one loaded brush. He will make three marks, paint the floor, then paint himself. That wants a towel under it rather than an intervention.

insight.headline: A large collaborative piece teaches something a small one can't.
paras: On a sheet of printer paper Azlyn owns every mark, and the work stops when she decides it is finished. The three of you on six feet of paper changes the terms. Her line runs into your line, somebody paints over her best bit, and the thing on the floor at the end belongs to nobody in particular. Three-year-olds play alongside each other more than with each other, and a shared surface is one of the few ways to move that on without a lesson about sharing. She gets a result that came out of three pairs of hands and could not have come out of one.

days.safety: Washable non-toxic paint only, because Kreston will get a loaded brush into his mouth at some point in the hour. Wet paint on a hard floor is slippery, so keep everybody kneeling and wipe spills as they happen. The walk to the store runs in open sun, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you. Two open cups of water sit at floor level for the whole hour, so tape them down on the wall side of your place and hers, out past where Kreston kneels, and tip them into the sink the moment the brushes go down.

days.title: The Instrument Museum
days.prepTonight: Clear one table end to end and put the thick card, the crayons, the marker, the string and a shoebox on the chair beside it.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Museum of Things That Make a Sound

opening.title: Six Things Worth Showing
opening.need: a laundry basket · 6 things from round the house that make a sound.
steps: Walk her through every room with the basket and let her choose things that make a noise. A colander, a tin of beans, a bunch of keys, a comb. Nothing breakable.
Stop her at six. Six fits the table; the rest go back where they came from.
Sit on the floor and play each one once. She puts them in order, best last, and that order lays the table out at quarter past nine.

main.title: The Museum of Things That Make a Sound
materials: Thick card, 6 pieces for labels and 1 large piece for the sign
steps: Set the six along the table with a hand's width between them, in her order, and stand the one she rated best on the shoebox.
Fold each label card in half so it stands up. She draws the object on the front in crayon; you write her words underneath, word for word.
Take the big piece of card for the sign. She names her museum, you write the name in marker, and it goes on the wall above the table.
Tape the string along the front edge of the table, end to end, at table height. That is the line visitors stand behind.
Run a strip of masking tape on the floor a stride back from the string. Visitors stand on the tape; she stands on the museum side.
Be the first visitor. Stand on the tape, hands behind your back, and let her show you one exhibit. Ask one question and no more.
main.tip: Write her labels down wrong. "It is a shaker and it is Kreston's and it is loud" beats a tidy caption.

outside.title: The Stick That Rings
paras: Yesterday was about what each thing sounds like. Today is about how long it keeps sounding after the hand comes off. One tap on the lamp post, then everybody counts out loud until it goes quiet, and she says the number she got to. The same tap on a wooden gate stops the count at one. Rank three things by their number on the way home, longest ringer first, and bring the stick in for the museum.

days.infant: Kreston is 14 months and copies what he sees. Hand him a stick at the gate and he will hit it where you hit it. He has three to five words now, so name the gate every time you pass it.

second.title: Azlyn Gives the Tour
second.intro: She runs the museum all afternoon, and every person in the house comes through as a visitor who knows nothing.
materials: The finished museum: 6 exhibits, 6 labels, the sign, the string, the shoebox plinth
1 or 2 teddies, as the first audience
Your phone, to film the last run
steps: Lay the cushions on the floor behind the tape line.
Sit the teddies on them for the first tour. She works out what to say with nobody watching.
Come in as a visitor. Knock, wait to be let in, sit on a cushion. Stay in role when she tells you the colander is a drum, because today it is.
She walks the six in order and plays every one, reading her labels back from memory rather than off the card.
Ask one real question at the end. "Which is the loudest?" and let her prove it.
Film the last tour for Joseph, start to finish, no directing from behind the camera.
Take the string down the moment the tours are over and lift the small exhibits onto a high shelf.
second.tip: Do not prompt her through it. Long gaps are her assembling the next sentence, and filling the gap hands the tour back to you.

alternatives: Two exhibits and one visitor, on the sofa.
Six soft things instead, and a museum you are allowed to touch.
Draw the museum on paper instead of building it.
Give the tour down the phone to somebody who is not in the house.
outAgain: The woods loop, and collect six things for a museum of outdoor sounds
The riverside path in the shade, the coolest hour of the day
The park with a bucket, hunting for one thing that rings
The hardware store, to run a hand along the chains and the pipes
The thrift store, hunting one instrument to go on the museum table
days.krestonPM: Bring him through as a visitor on your hip so nothing comes off the table. At 14 months he points at what he wants, and it will be the same exhibit three times running. Let Azlyn lift it down and play it for him.

insight.headline: Explaining it to a stranger sends her back through it another way.
paras: Answering a question needs a fragment. Explaining six objects to a visitor who knows nothing needs an order, a reason for the order, and words that work for somebody who was not there when she chose them. Teachers call it the protégé effect: preparing to teach a thing sends you back through it by another route. The studies behind it ran with older children, and the shape of it is on your kitchen floor this afternoon. Azlyn will say more than any question of yours could get out of her, and in longer sentences. Sit on the cushion and be a stranger. The tour goes further the less you help.

days.safety: The string barrier comes down and goes in a drawer the moment the tours finish. String at toddler height is a strangulation risk and it never stays up overnight. The small exhibits, keys and anything that fits in a mouth go up high before Kreston is loose in the room. The walk runs down an open street, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

days.title: Real Tools
days.prepTonight: Empty a cookie tin and stand it on the table with the sandpaper and a wooden ruler or paint stirrer, and put the screwdriver, the two screws and the rubber bands in a lidded tub in the drawer. The screwdriver comes out at eight, the screws and the bands at quarter past nine.

schedule.name: Hanging the Tins on the Fence

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Sweeping Song and the Wiping Song

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: The Carrots and the Real Peeler

opening.title: The Two Tools We Need
opening.need: 1 real screwdriver · 1 square of sandpaper · 1 wooden ruler or paint stirrer.
steps: Put the screwdriver and the sandpaper on the table and name them both. She holds one at a time, sitting down, and hands it back before she gets the other.
Show her the wrist turn in the air, right hand, elbow tucked in. Twenty slow turns of nothing, and say which way tightens.
Hand her the sandpaper and the ruler and let her rub the ends until nothing catches your thumb.

main.title: Building the Box Guitar
materials: 1 cookie tin, or a sturdy shoebox
2 screws or cup hooks (substitute: 2 pencils taped under the bands as bridges)
1 wooden ruler or paint stirrer, sanded, for the neck
steps: Tape the sanded ruler along the top of the tin, three turns of masking tape, so a hand's length sticks out past the end as a neck.

Start each screw yourself, a few turns into the soft wood, one near each end of where the bands will sit. Hand her the screwdriver and let her drive them home, until each head stands a finger's width proud. Sandpaper any splinter that lifts.
If the wood is too hard for her to turn, tape a pencil flat across the tin at each end as the bridges.
Stretch the three rubber bands around the tin and up over the screw heads, thickest first. Take the screwdriver back and put it in the drawer.
Pluck each band in turn with her. Thick and slack gives the low note, thin and tight the high one.
Wind one band twice round a screw to tighten it and pluck again. Let her do the next one, and let her stretch one until it pings off.
main.tip: Let her fail at the screw for a good thirty seconds before you steady the tin.

outside.title: Hanging the Tins on the Fence
paras: Push three empty tins upside down over three fence posts, spaced along the run. She walks the fence hitting them in order with the stick from yesterday, then walks back the other way. Move one tin to a different post and let her find the song moved with it.

days.infant: Kreston is 14 months. Put one tin on the grass for him and leave it there. He will hit it, sit on it, try to stack something on it and carry it off. The last is the newest: he would rather move a thing than keep it still.

second.title: The Sweeping Song and the Wiping Song
second.intro: Three real jobs, three real songs, and the job finishes when the song does. The house is tidier at half past two than it was at one.
materials: 2 cloths and 1 bowl of warm water
The box guitar from this morning
A phone or radio for music
steps: Pick three songs with her and put them in order: a fast one, a slow one, and one she asks for. Play ten seconds of each.
Fast song, kitchen floor. She sweeps into the pan, you hold it, and the crumbs go in the trash before the song ends.
Slow song, low surfaces. One cloth each, wrung out in the warm water. She does the cabinet doors and the chair legs at her height, you do the table.
Her song, the laundry basket. She carries it to the clothes and sorts everything into piles by who it belongs to.
Let her choose a fourth song and one more job of her own picking. Do it with her.
Sit down on the clean floor when the last song ends and look at what changed.
Fetch the box guitar and play one more song with no job hanging off it. She built the thing this morning and she has not heard it in a room this quiet.
second.tip: Length of song sets length of job, so a two-minute song against a five-minute job is a broken deal. Match them.

alternatives: One song, one job, and the rest of the afternoon in the yard.
Sort the whole clean wash into piles and stop there.
Wash the plastic plates in a bowl of warm water outside.
Play the box guitar along to three songs and leave the jobs until tomorrow.
outAgain: Swimming, and the coolest room she will stand in today
The paddling pool at home if the session is full
The splash pad, and take an extra towel
The shady woods loop, if the pool is shut for the changeover
The park at five, once the heat is off the equipment
days.krestonPM: He swims too. At 14 months he walks down the shallow steps holding the rail rather than being carried in, which is worth the ten minutes it costs. Hold him under the arms and let him kick one length. Get him out and dressed before he is cold, which comes sooner than it looks.

insight.headline: Real tools and real jobs beat toy versions, every time.
paras: A plastic screwdriver turns nothing, and Azlyn knows the difference by the weight of it in her hand. The real one bites, resists, and rewards her the moment the screw starts to turn, a feedback loop no toy version gives her. The same holds for the broom and the peeler: real work has a result somebody notices. A household job she has been trusted with holds her longer than an activity built to entertain her, because the job was going to happen either way. You supervise the tool and let her own the outcome, and today the outcome is a guitar that plays and a floor that is clean.

days.safety: Loose screws and rubber bands are choking hazards and both sit at Kreston's exact height. Count them out and count them back in. The screwdriver goes back in the drawer between turns, never left on the table, and the peeler stays in your hand alongside hers for every single carrot. The fence run is in open sun, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: The Circle Games
days.prepTonight: Push the living room furniture back to the walls and leave the masking tape, a cushion for each person and the jar of rice in the middle of the floor.

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Two Library Books on the Sofa

opening.title: A Cushion for Everyone
opening.need: masking tape · 1 cushion per person, Kreston included.
steps: Lay a circle of masking tape on the floor, big enough for everyone to sit on the line with their feet inside it. Let her walk it round while you stick it down.
She counts the people in the house and fetches that many cushions. Count them onto the tape together and send her back if the number is short.
She decides who sits where and puts each cushion down herself. Kreston's goes next to hers, because it always does.

main.title: The Sound That Goes Round
materials: 1 roll masking tape, for the circle on the floor
1 shaker, or 1 jar of rice taped shut
steps: Everybody sits on a cushion on the tape. One rule for the whole hour: the sound travels one way round the circle and never jumps across the middle.
Start with a clap. You clap once, the person on your left claps once, and it goes round until it comes back to you. Three times.
Add the shaker. One shake each, passed hand to hand, and nobody shakes it out of turn. She will police this harder than you do.
Pass the beanbag round instead. Whoever holds it makes any sound at all, and the next person copies it before passing it on.
Add the bell, and it stays in your hand. You ring it once to end a round and everybody stops dead, so the bell never travels. Ring it after a different number of passes each time.
Give her the beanbag last and let her invent the sound everybody copies. Get it wrong on purpose once and let her correct you.
main.tip: Sit on the floor rather than on a chair at the edge. A circle works while every face in it is at the same height.

outside.title: The Circle of Found Things
paras: Scuff a big circle in the dry dirt with your heel, in the yard or on a bare patch of the park. Fill it with what the first of September has on the ground: dry grass seed heads, a green walnut husk, a curled leaf, a feather, a strip of bark. She lays each thing on the line rather than in a heap. Walk the outside once, naming the row.

days.infant: Kreston is 14 months and stacks two blocks. Out here he will lift things off her circle and put them down somewhere else, the same sorting instinct arriving a year behind hers. Give him his own small circle scuffed beside hers and the big strips of bark and curled leaves to move into it. Nuts and seed heads stay in your hand.

second.title: Whoever Holds the Spoon Sings
second.intro: One wooden spoon decides who sings. The circle is still taped on the floor with the cushions on it, and the rule sits in somebody's hand.
materials: The taped circle and the cushions
Paper and a pen, for the list of who chose what
steps: Spread the blanket flat in the middle of the circle. The spoon lives there between turns, a place to put it down that is nobody's.
Set the rule out loud once: whoever holds the spoon chooses the song, everybody sings it with them, and nobody starts a song while the spoon is on the blanket.
First time round, one song each. Take a short one yourself so she sees the shape of a turn.
Write the list on the paper as you go, name then song, in her hearing. She will start choosing with an eye on how it looks written down.
Second time round, everybody stands and the person with the spoon adds one action the rest copy.
Put the spoon in Kreston's hand for a turn. He holds it, everybody waits, and somebody sings what he likes.
Read the list back at the end and let her pick which one finishes the afternoon.
second.tip: Sing loud and sing out of tune. She stops joining in the second the singing turns into a performance she thinks she could get wrong.

alternatives: Two people, one spoon, three songs, on the sofa.
Draw round the cushions on paper and make a map of who sat where.
Sing the list again at bedtime with the lights out.
Pass the spoon round and take turns naming animals instead of singing.
outAgain: The library, every two weeks, and hunt the shelf for songbooks with the words in
Indoor playground, if story time has finished and the place is packed
The park on the walk back, and the bench in the shade
The market square, where somebody is often playing something
Home the long way, singing the list again
days.krestonPM: Sit him in the board-book corner and let Azlyn choose his book and carry it to the desk. At 14 months he points at pictures and waits for you to name them, and he will point at the same dog on every page. Name it every time.

insight.headline: Sitting in a circle changes how a group talks.
paras: A circle puts everybody at the same height with nobody at the head of the table, and a three-year-old reads that arrangement fast. Azlyn can see every face at once, so she picks up whose turn is coming without being told, and a shared object like the spoon makes the invisible rule visible. Preschools have run circle time for a century for reasons that hold up: turn-taking, joint attention, and a group small enough that her contribution lands. You do not need to run it like a teacher. You need to sit on the floor and take your turn when it comes.

days.safety: The bell is choke-sized and Kreston is sitting in the circle, so it stays in your hand for the whole game and every round ends from there. Count it in and count it out. Check the jar lid is taped tight before the shaker moves at all, because a jar of loose rice is the same hazard spread thin, and swap to a solid shaker if the tape lifts. Outside, everything he is handed has to be bigger than his mouth, so he gets bark and big leaves, and you kneel between him and Azlyn's circle to keep the gravel, the seed heads and the walnut husk on her side of you. September sun still burns, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

days.title: The Shadow Concert
days.prepTonight: Take the shade off a lamp and stand it by the wall with the white sheet, the clothespins and two dining chairs.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Shadow That Grows and Shrinks

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Her Shadow at Half Past Ten

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: Everybody Gets a Turn in the Light

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: Putting the Market Fruit in the Bowl

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: Her Own Shadow on the Wall

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Bath, Then the Film of the Show

opening.title: The Sheet and the Lamp
opening.need: 1 white sheet or a plain shower curtain · 2 chairs · 6 clothespins or bulldog clips.
steps: Stand the two chairs back to back, a long stride apart, in the middle of the room.
Drape the sheet over both backs so it hangs to the floor and let her clip it, three pegs a chair. Pull the bottom edge straight.
Stand the lamp on the floor behind it, switched off, and make her wait until quarter past nine.

main.title: The Shadow That Grows and Shrinks
materials: 1 white sheet or plain shower curtain, hung between 2 chairs
1 lamp with the shade off, or 1 bright flashlight
1 roll masking tape, to mark the floor where she stood
A phone or radio for music
steps: Shut the curtains, check the six clothespins are still gripping, and stand the lamp on the floor behind the sheet, two or three strides back so there is room to walk between them. Tape the cable flat to the floor from lamp to socket.
Big light off, lamp on. Send her behind the sheet and sit down in front.

Have her walk towards the lamp a step at a time while you say what her shadow is doing. It swells until it fills the sheet and blurs at the edges. Stop her a long arm's length short of the bulb and tape a mark on the floor there.
Walk her back until she almost touches the sheet. She comes out small and sharp, her own size, and the second tape mark goes there.
Music on, and she moves between the two marks however the song asks. Call out what you can see from the front, because she cannot.
Swap. She sits out front, you go behind, and she says which mark to stand on to be a giant.
main.tip: She controls the size with her feet. Say "come towards the lamp" rather than "make it bigger".

outside.title: Her Shadow at Half Past Ten
paras: Stand her still on the path at half past ten. Put one stone at the top of her shadow's head and another at her heels, then measure the gap in her own footsteps. Come back before dinner, stand her on the same spot facing the same way, and put a third stone down.

days.infant: Kreston is 14 months and has three to five words. Stand him in the sun beside her and he may notice the dark shape moving with him, or walk through hers without a glance. Hold his hand, step forward together, and say "shadow".

second.title: Everybody Gets a Turn in the Light
second.intro: The sheet stays up and the person behind it changes every few minutes.
materials: The sheet and the lamp, set up as this morning
2 craft sticks or pencils, and masking tape
Paper and a pen, for the running order
A phone or radio for music
steps: She draws two shapes on the thick card, big and simple, a bird and a moon or whatever she asks. You cut them out while she holds it flat.
Tape a craft stick to the back of each so it can be held up from below, clear of a hand.
Lay the cushions in a row in front of the sheet.
Write the running order with her and let her announce each name before that person goes behind.
Music on. One turn each, one song each, and anybody who would rather not dance holds a card shape up into the light instead.
Give her the last turn and let her use both card shapes and her own body at once.
Film that turn from the audience side and watch it back with her at bath time.
second.tip: Applaud every turn the same, Kreston's included. An unequal round is what she brings up at bedtime.

alternatives: Hand shadows on the wall by flashlight, no sheet at all.
Six card shapes and a show with no dancing in it.
Take the sheet down and do it outside in the low sun.
Draw round her shadow on paper taped to the wall and color it in.
outAgain: The market, and she picks the fruit that goes in the bowl at four o'clock
The produce market and the bakery, one thing carried by her
The park on the way back, once the shadows are getting long
A shady bench, something cold, ten minutes of watching people
The woods loop at five, where the low sun lays stripes across the path
days.krestonPM: He gets a turn behind the sheet on your hip, with somebody out front telling him what he looks like. At 14 months he will reach for the lamp, so keep it short. At the market give him one thing to carry to the bag.

insight.headline: She's met shadows three times now, and each time added something.
paras: In February she made animals on a sheet by flashlight and swelled a fox up the fabric by walking him at the flashlight, with the shadow still a thing her hands held. In the summer she found her own on the hot sidewalk and worked out it belonged to her. Today the shadow that changes size is her whole body, and her feet are the control. Concepts arrive in layers at three, months apart, through the same material met in a new arrangement. Nothing was wasted in February and nothing is finished today. She will meet shadows again in December when the sun is low all day.

days.safety: A lamp bulb with the shade off gets hot enough to scorch the sheet and hot enough to burn a hand, so stand it two or three strides back and keep the fabric a long arm's length clear of it at the closest. The tape mark nearest the lamp is as close as anybody goes, Azlyn included, and she walks up to it rather than past it. Tape the cable flat to the floor along its whole run, and stand the lamp where Kreston cannot pull it down on himself. Standing still on an open path at half past ten is ten minutes of direct sun, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you.
